## Wooden Rails and Horse Power

The railway began as a way of moving heavy things along the ground with less effort than a road allowed. Before anyone thought of a locomotive, the problem was friction. A cart on a rutted track needs a great deal of force to start and keep moving, and most of that force is lost to the uneven surface, the wheels sinking into mud, and the wheel rims dragging against the ground. If the wheel runs on a smooth, hard, level surface, the same load can be moved with a fraction of the effort. Mine operators in central Europe worked this out first, and the earliest railways were, in essence, carefully laid tracks inside and around mines.

The evidence for these early tracks is partial but consistent. By the sixteenth century, wooden rails guided wagons out of German and Central European mines, and Georgius Agricola's *De Re Metallica*, published in 1556, included illustrations of small wagons running on timber tracks carrying ore and waste. The wagons were pushed by hand or drawn by horses, and the wooden rails were usually laid as two parallel beams, sometimes capped with strips of iron to reduce wear. The flanged wheel, which kept the vehicle on the track without a driver steering it, appeared in these settings. The idea was simple enough that it spread quickly wherever heavy bulk materials had to be moved over short distances: coal from pits to a river or harbour, stone from quarries to a building site, and ore from mines to smelters.

In Britain, the coal trade provided the strongest pressure. The coalfields of the North East, around Newcastle and the River Tyne, were far from the great consumers of coal in London, but they were close to the sea. The problem was getting coal from the pit mouth to the riverside staithes where it could be loaded onto colliers. Horses pulled wagons along wooden wagonways in the seventeenth century, and by the eighteenth the network had grown into an intricate system of lines feeding the river. Wooden rails wore out quickly under heavy loads, and in the 1760s and 1770s iron began to replace timber. Early cast iron rails were brittle, and the first iron plateways, with flat rails and flanged wheels on the vehicle, were built in the 1760s and 1770s. The Caldon Low tramway in Staffordshire, opened in 1776, is often cited as one of the first public iron-railed lines in Britain, serving the limestone and iron trades.

The engineering of these lines was ambitious for their time. Builders learned to level gradients, cut through hillsides, and cross valleys on embankments and timber trestles. They also began to standardise. Gauges, the distance between rails, varied from one line to another, and a wagon built for one colliery might not run on the track of its neighbour. This variation was not yet a serious problem, because each line was a closed system serving a single owner. It would become a serious problem later, when the lines were joined.

Horses were the motive power of this early era, and they were enormously effective on level track. A single horse could pull a much heavier load along an iron rail than it could along a road. On steeper ground, horses were used in teams or replaced by fixed engines that wound wagons up inclines with cables. Stationary steam engines, first the atmospheric engines of Thomas Newcomen and then the improved, condensing engines of James Watt, were applied to hauling cable on inclines by the late eighteenth century. This combination of horse on the level and engine on the hill became the standard practice of the tramway age, and it explains why steam was used on railways in a fixed role long before it moved on wheels.

The social character of these early lines is worth noting. Many were private, built by mine owners, canal companies, ironworks, or landowners to serve their own enterprises. The horses and the men who drove them were employed by the owner, and the wagons carried the owner's products. Some lines carried passengers as well, though this was an incidental use for most of the eighteenth century. A few of the more prominent tramways, such as the one built by Ralph Allen to carry stone from his quarries near Bath, or the Surrey Iron Railway of 1803, which operated as a public carrier, showed that a track could serve many customers. The Surrey line is often cited as the first public railway, and it charged tolls to any operator who put a vehicle on its rails, anticipating the common-carrier principle that later railways would adopt.

By the early nineteenth century, then, the basic elements of the railway were in place: a prepared track, flanged wheels, a method of guiding vehicles, and a motive power that could be supplied by animals or fixed engines. What was missing was a self-propelled engine that could travel on the rails and pull a train without a stationary engine at each end or a horse at every wagon. The problem was waiting for steam to become light enough and strong enough to move on wheels.

## The First Locomotives

The steam engine was born as a machine for pumping water out of mines, and its early forms were heavy, slow, and inefficient. Newcomen's engine of around 1712 used steam at atmospheric pressure, condensed it to create a vacuum, and let the atmosphere push a piston down. It was a workable pump but a poor prime mover, consuming large amounts of coal for modest output. James Watt's separate condenser, developed in the 1760s and perfected in the following decades, greatly improved fuel economy, and his double-acting engine with a rotary motion made the steam engine useful for driving machinery in mills and factories. Watt's engines were built to very close tolerances and were expensive, and his firm was strict about licensing. The higher-pressure steam engines that could be made smaller and lighter came from a different line of development, associated with Richard Trevithick in Cornwall and with makers who worked outside Watt's patents.

Trevithick is generally credited with building the first steam locomotive to run on rails. In 1801 he built a road carriage that ran on the streets of Camborne, and in 1804 he built a locomotive for the Penydarren ironworks in South Wales. On 21 February 1804, the engine hauled a load of iron, reportedly around ten tons, along a plateway in the Merthyr Tydfil area, carrying a group of men as well. The journey took several hours and the engine was damaged by its own weight, since the cast iron rails of the period were not strong enough to bear the locomotive for long. The experiment proved that steam could move on rails, but it also revealed the problems that would occupy engineers for two decades: weak track, poor adhesion between wheel and rail, and a boiler and engine that were too heavy for the infrastructure.

Adhesion was a particular concern. Engineers initially feared that smooth wheels on smooth rails would slip and spin rather than pull. Some designers tried to solve this by using cogged rails or rack systems. John Blenkinsop, a colliery manager at Middleton near Leeds, took out a patent in 1811 for a rack railway, in which a toothed rail engaged a cogwheel on the locomotive. Blenkinsop's engines, built by Matthew Murray, went into service at Middleton Colliery in 1812, and they worked for years, carrying coal on a track that had been fitted with a toothed rail along one side. The rack solution was overkill for a level route, but it demonstrated that a steam engine could haul a useful load on a railway. Blenkinsop's engine also had a flaw that would become a recurring theme in early locomotive design: its wheels were driven by cogs, and the mechanism was heavier and more complicated than it needed to be.

The breakthrough came from the North East, where the coalfields had both the traffic and the engineers. William Hedley at Wylam Colliery built *Puffing Billy* in 1813 or 1814, a locomotive with its cylinders connected to the wheels by gearing. It had enough adhesion to pull coal wagons on a smooth rail, which was a significant result: it showed that the weight of the engine itself was sufficient to grip the rail on a level track. Hedley's engine has survived, and it is preserved in the Science Museum in London. Its success encouraged other colliery engineers to build engines, and the most important of them was George Stephenson, the enginewright at Killingworth Colliery.

Stephenson's *Blücher*, built in 1814 for the Killingworth wagonway, was the first locomotive he built that could pull a train of loaded wagons with reasonable reliability. It had a single pair of cylinders and drove its wheels through connecting rods rather than gears, a design that proved far more practical. Stephenson went on to build several locomotives for collieries and for the Killingworth line, and he learned from each. His engines were not elegant, and early in his career he was regarded as a practical mechanic rather than a scientist. But he understood the relationship between boiler size, steam production, and power output, and he saw that a locomotive would work best with a boiler that produced steam faster than the cylinders could use it. His engineering judgment, combined with an ability to attract financial backers, made him the central figure of the next phase.

Stephenson's most famous early achievement was the Stockton and Darlington Railway, opened on 27 September 1825. The line was promoted by Quaker businessmen in Darlington who wanted to carry coal from the inland collieries to the sea at Stockton. Its original plan was largely horse-drawn, and steam was introduced by the promoters at Stephenson's urging. The engine that opened the line, *Locomotion No. 1*, hauled a train that carried coal wagons and, in a concession to the crowd, a number of passenger carriages. The line did not use steam exclusively; horses continued to haul many trains for years. It did, however, show that the locomotive could work on an ordinary railway and that the public would pay to ride behind one.

The Stockton and Darlington was not a passenger railway in the modern sense. It was a mineral line with a passenger service added on. The idea of a railway built primarily for passengers, linking two major centres of population and industry, was developed in the late 1820s by people who saw that the railway could be much more than a colliery tool. That idea would be tested at Rainhill, and then on a line between Liverpool and Manchester.

## Liverpool, Manchester, and the Rainhill Trials

Liverpool and Manchester were the two largest commercial centres in the north-west of England in the 1820s. Liverpool was the port through which raw cotton entered Britain and through which Manchester's manufactured textiles left for export. Their connection was by road and by canal, and the canal was congested and slow. The promoters of a railway between the two cities argued that a faster link would benefit both, and they found support among merchants, manufacturers, and landowners who were willing to invest. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was authorised by Parliament in 1826 after a bitter fight with canal and landed interests, and its construction was supervised by George Stephenson with his son Robert, who had trained in engineering and would later become a significant locomotive designer himself.

The line was engineered to a higher standard than anything that had been built before. Stephenson and his colleagues carried it across Chat Moss, a large peat bog that had defeated earlier attempts to cross it, by floating the track on a bed of brushwood and earth. They cut through rock at Olive Mount and built a series of embankments and cuttings. The line needed a locomotive capable of reliable operation over a long distance with passengers and freight, and the directors decided to hold a competition to choose the motive power. The competition, known as the Rainhill Trials, took place in October 1829 on a flat section of the line near Rainhill.

The rules set by the directors were demanding. Locomotives had to haul a specified load over a set distance, carry a minimum weight, and maintain a minimum speed. They had to be light enough to avoid damaging the track and had to consume their own fuel and water. Several entries were submitted. Some were rejected for failing to meet the weight limit, and some broke down during the trials. The competitors included Timothy Hackworth's *Sans Pareil*, John Ericsson and John Braithwaite's *Novelty*, and a vertical-boilered machine from Burstall. George and Robert Stephenson's *Rocket* was the winning entry. It had a multitubular boiler, a suggestion attributed to Henry Booth, the company's secretary, which passed hot gases through many small tubes in the water-filled boiler, greatly increasing the heating surface and the steam output. The *Rocket* was fast, reliable, and capable of the required load, and it won the prize of £500.

The Rainhill Trials were a turning point for several reasons. They established the design of the locomotive that would serve for decades: a boiler with a fire-tube arrangement, cylinders mounted at an angle, and a driving wheel connected to a coupling rod. They also established the principle that a railway could be operated by a selection of machines chosen for performance, rather than by a fixed design imposed by an engineer. The winning engine was not perfect. It rode badly at speed and had a tendency to be unstable, but it showed that steam could meet the demands of a public railway.

The line opened on 15 September 1830 with a ceremony that is remembered for its tragedy. William Huskisson, the Member of Parliament for Liverpool and a prominent supporter of the railway, had been invited to attend. The train stopped at Parkside to take on water, and passengers were permitted to leave the carriages and walk along the track. Huskisson stepped onto the track as the *Rocket* approached from the other direction, and he was struck by the engine. He was taken to hospital in Eccles, but he died there that evening. His death was a shock and was widely reported, and it did little to slow the growth of the railway. The line carried passengers and goods in large numbers from the start, and it became the model for trunk lines that followed.

The Liverpool and Manchester was also a commercial success. It attracted far more passengers than its promoters had predicted, and it carried cotton and other goods at a fraction of the earlier cost. Its success convinced investors that railways were a sound investment, and it provoked a wave of proposals for new lines across the country. Within a decade, Britain had developed a national railway network, although the process was far from orderly. The railway had moved from a niche industrial technology to the centre of economic life.

## The Railway Mania and the Gauge Question

The late 1830s and 1840s saw an explosion of railway construction in Britain. Investors, many of them small savers, were drawn by the prospect of high dividends, and promoters proposed lines across the country with little regard for whether they were needed or whether they could be financed. Parliament authorised hundreds of schemes, and the stock market fuelled a speculative boom that historians call Railway Mania. The peak came in 1845 and 1846, when Parliament received plans for many thousands of miles of new track. The bubble burst in 1847 when the financial system tightened, many schemes collapsed, and investors lost substantial sums. Even so, the mania left Britain with a dense network of lines, and many of the routes that survive today were built in these years.

The mania also produced a dispute that is one of the most important episodes in railway history: the gauge war. Early railways had used various track widths, but the most common was the gauge used by Stephenson's lines, roughly four feet eight and a half inches. Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the engineer of the Great Western Railway, chose a much wider gauge of seven feet and a quarter inch. Brunel believed that a wider gauge would give greater stability and higher speeds, and that it would allow larger carriages and more powerful locomotives. The Great Western ran broad gauge trains between London and Bristol, and its engines and carriages were among the most impressive of the period. Brunel's gauge also had strong advocates, and for a time it seemed that Britain might have two incompatible systems.

The incompatibility was a serious problem. Goods and passengers had to be transferred at the boundaries between broad and standard gauge lines, and that transfer was slow, costly, and inconvenient. Commercial interests and the government came to see the mixed gauges as an obstacle to national efficiency. A Royal Commission was appointed in 1845 to consider the issue, and it recommended that the standard gauge be adopted for the country's railways. Parliament passed the Gauge Act in 1846, which made the standard gauge the required width for new lines, with some exceptions for lines that already used broad gauge. The Great Western continued to operate broad gauge for decades, and the last broad gauge trains ran in 1892, when the company converted its lines. The gauge war was a lesson in how a technical choice could be decided by politics and commerce as much as by engineering merit.

The mania also led to regulation. The Railway Regulation Act of 1844, often called the Gladstone Act after William Gladstone, who was then President of the Board of Trade, established a system of oversight for new railways. It required companies to provide cheap third-class travel on some services, and it gave the state the right to purchase railways after a set period. The Act was not fully enforced, but it marked the beginning of the state's interest in the railway as a public service. Later legislation would strengthen this role, establishing inspectorates and standards for safety and for the conduct of companies.

Many of the companies that emerged from the mania were later combined into larger units. By the middle of the nineteenth century, the British railway system had consolidated into a small number of major companies, each serving a region. These companies competed fiercely for traffic, and they built duplicate lines to the same towns, sometimes at great cost. Consolidation continued until the Railways Act of 1921 grouped the lines into four large companies, which came into effect on 1 January 1923: the London, Midland and Scottish; the London and North Eastern; the Great Western; and the Southern. The grouping reflected a long struggle between competition and rationalisation, and it provided the basis for the nationalised system that would be created after the Second World War.

## Railways Across Europe

While Britain was building its network, the railway was spreading across the Continent. The first lines in continental Europe were short, often built by private investors or by state engineers who wanted to show that the technology could work. Saint-Étienne to Andrézieux, opened in 1827 in France, was a horse-worked line that carried coal, and its engineer Marc Seguin later built steam locomotives. Germany's first public railway, between Nuremberg and Fürth, opened in 1835 and carried passengers with a locomotive named *Adler*, built in England by Robert Stephenson and Company. Belgium opened a line between Brussels and Mechelen in the same year, and its government took an early and active role in building a national network. France's first main line, from Paris to Saint-Germain, opened in 1837, and it was followed by lines to Versailles and then to the coast.

The governments of Continental states often took a more active role than the British had. In Belgium, the state built the first main lines and then operated them, creating a centralised system that would become a model for much of Europe. In Prussia, the state supported railway construction as part of a strategy to unify and strengthen the country. Railways made it possible to move troops quickly, to supply armies at a distance, and to link the parts of a country that had been separated by distance and poor roads. Military planners understood this well, and railway development became entangled with national policy. The German states built a network that was intended, from the start, to serve national goals, and the Prussian General Staff became deeply interested in the planning of lines and junctions.

Russia built its first railway in 1837, a line from St Petersburg to the imperial residence at Tsarskoye Selo. It was short, but it demonstrated that a large and sparsely populated empire could use the railway. The Russian government commissioned foreign engineers to design and build longer lines, and the first major trunk line, between St Petersburg and Moscow, was completed in 1851. The vast distances of the Russian empire made the railway an obvious tool for economic and military integration, and its later development would culminate in the Trans-Siberian Railway, built between 1891 and 1916, which linked Moscow with Vladivostok on the Pacific. The construction of that line was one of the greatest engineering undertakings of its age, crossing permafrost, mountains, and wide rivers.

The Austro-Hungarian Empire built a network that reflected its geography and its politics. Lines were built from Vienna into Bohemia, Moravia, and the Alpine provinces, and the empire's engineers had to overcome mountain barriers that were formidable even by the standards of the day. The Semmering line, opened in 1854, crossed the Semmering Pass in the eastern Alps and used a series of tunnels, viaducts, and sharp curves. It was a pioneering project in mountain railway engineering and is still in use. The Alps, which divided Italy from the north and Switzerland from its neighbours, were a barrier that railway engineers had to solve, and the solutions they found would shape the future of European rail travel.

In Italy, the railway developed slowly at first, held back by political division before unification in 1861. Once the country was united, the government built lines to connect the major cities and then to link the north with the south. Italy's railways were later electrified early and extensively, partly because the country had few coal fields and depended on imported fuel. The Valtellina line, electrified in 1902, was one of the first main lines in Europe to use electric traction, and it was the forerunner of many electrified routes that would follow.

Spain and Portugal built their railways in the mid-nineteenth century with substantial foreign investment. Spain adopted a broad gauge of about 1.67 metres, partly as a defensive measure against foreign invasion by rail, and that gauge persists in much of the country's network today, which later created problems for the country's high-speed lines. The Spanish experience shows that the choice of gauge could have consequences for generations, and that it was sometimes made for reasons unrelated to the efficiency of operation.

Across Europe, the railway changed the pattern of daily life. Cities expanded along the lines, and towns that were on the railway grew faster than those that were not. Passenger travel became cheaper and more frequent, and the middle classes began to take holidays at distant resorts that the railway had brought within reach. Newspapers, letters, and goods moved faster, and the time it took to travel between cities fell sharply. The railway also changed the perception of time. Before the railway, local time varied from town to town, and each community kept its own clock by the sun. As the railway required timetables that could be followed across many stations, the need for uniform time became urgent. Britain and other countries gradually adopted standard time, and the railway was among the main reasons for the change.

## The Americas

The United States adopted the railway with great enthusiasm, and it developed a railway system larger and faster than any in Europe. The first American railways were built in the 1820s, and the most important early line was the Baltimore and Ohio, chartered in 1827 to connect the port of Baltimore with the Ohio River and the interior. The Baltimore and Ohio was intended to compete with the Erie Canal, which had opened in 1825 and made New York the dominant port of the interior. The B&O's early engines were a mixture of imported and domestic designs, and the company experimented with horses, sails, and even gravity before choosing steam.

The B&O's *Tom Thumb*, built by Peter Cooper in 1830, was a small locomotive that demonstrated the potential of steam on American tracks. Cooper's engine was a modest machine with a vertical boiler, and in a famous demonstration it was raced against a horse-drawn car. The engine was ahead for much of the course, but its drive belt slipped and the horse won. The story is often told as a joke at the expense of early steam, but it also shows that the first American locomotives were light machines built to prove a concept, and that the engineers were learning as they went. The South Carolina Canal and Railroad Company's *Best Friend of Charleston*, which began regular operation in December 1830, was the first American locomotive to haul a passenger train in regular service. Its boiler exploded in 1831, which led the company to abandon steam for a time, but the episode did not stop the spread of the American locomotive.

American railways developed their own distinctive engineering. The American locomotive of the nineteenth century often had a leading truck, a small set of wheels in front of the driving wheels, which allowed the engine to negotiate curves on the lightly built track of the frontier. The American engine also had a large smokestack with a spark-arresting screen, a headlamp, and a cowcatcher, a sloping frame at the front designed to clear livestock from the track. American railroads built on a vast scale, often with cheap construction, long distances between stations, and light track that could be extended quickly across unsettled land. The American approach was pragmatic, and the railway became a means of settling and developing the continent.

The Civil War revealed the strategic value of railways. Both sides used rail to move troops and supplies, and lines in the Confederacy and the Union were fought over, damaged, and repaired repeatedly. The war accelerated the development of standardised equipment and of procedures for moving large numbers of troops. It also showed the importance of rail in linking the country, and it made the case for a transcontinental line that would connect the eastern states with California and the Pacific.

The Pacific Railroad Acts of 1862 and 1864 provided federal support for a railway from the Missouri River to the Pacific coast. The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento, and the Union Pacific built west from Omaha. The two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah, where a golden spike was driven on 10 May 1869. The project was supported by government loans and by grants of land along the route, which gave the railroads a stake in settlement and development. The Central Pacific depended heavily on Chinese labourers, who did much of the most dangerous work in the Sierra Nevada, and their contribution has been recognised in modern accounts of the project. The Union Pacific employed large numbers of Irish and other immigrant workers, and the completion of the line transformed the economics of the West.

The transcontinental railroad was followed by a rapid expansion of American railways. Dozens of companies built lines across the Midwest, the Great Plains, and the Mountain West, often with the encouragement of local governments and land speculators. The railroad companies sold land along their routes to settlers, and they built towns at intervals along the line, which became the centres of agricultural and commercial life. The result was a dense network that carried grain, cattle, lumber, coal, and manufactured goods. By the end of the nineteenth century, the United States had more railway mileage than the rest of the world combined, and the railroads were among the largest corporations in the country.

This expansion was not without problems. Competition among railroads led to rate wars, unstable prices, and financial failures. The Panic of 1873 bankrupted many lines and triggered a long depression. Farmers and shippers complained that railroads charged unfair rates, and they demanded government regulation. The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first federal regulatory agency in the United States, and it gave the government authority to oversee rates and practices. The Act was a significant step in the development of American regulation, and it set a pattern that would be followed in other industries.

The American railways also introduced many innovations that spread around the world. George Westinghouse patented the air brake in 1869, a system in which compressed air applied the brakes on every car of a train at once, making it possible to stop long trains safely. Before the air brake, brakemen had to run along the tops of cars and turn brake wheels by hand, a dangerous job that claimed many lives. Eli Janney patented the knuckle coupler in 1873, which coupled cars automatically when they were pushed together, removing the need for men to stand between cars to link them with pins. These devices made American railways safer and more productive, and they were later adopted worldwide. The Pullman sleeping car, developed by George Pullman in the 1860s, gave American long-distance travellers a level of comfort that European passengers rarely enjoyed, and it became a symbol of the luxury railway.

In 1883 the railroads of North America adopted a system of standard time zones, which they applied on 18 November of that year. Before that, each city kept its own local time, and railroad timetables were a confusing mixture of local times. The adoption of standard time was a remarkable act of coordination by private companies, and it was later made law by the federal government. The time zones were eventually adopted by the country and the rest of the world, and they remain the basis of civil timekeeping in much of the world.

Latin America built railways in the same period, often with British capital. Brazil's first railway, a line in Rio de Janeiro province promoted by Irineu Evangelista de Sousa, Baron of Mauá, opened in 1854. Argentina's railways were built in the 1850s and 1860s, and by the end of the century the country had a dense network linking the pampas with the port of Buenos Aires. Canada's first railway, the Champlain and St. Lawrence, opened in 1836 between Montreal and La Prairie. Canada later built a transcontinental line, the Canadian Pacific Railway, completed in 1885. In many Latin American countries, railways were built to export raw materials, and they connected interior producers with coastal ports rather than with each other, leaving a legacy that still shapes their networks.

## Asia, Africa, and Australia

The railway came to Asia and Africa primarily through colonial and commercial interests, and in many cases it was built to serve the needs of European powers rather than local populations. India's first railway opened on 16 April 1853, between Bombay and Thane, and it was followed by a rapid expansion of lines that served the cotton and grain trades, linked the interior with the ports, and carried British troops. The Indian network grew into one of the largest in the world, and it remains one of the busiest today. The gauge chosen for Indian railways was broader than the British standard, and the wide gauge reflects a decision that the British government made for reasons of cost and capacity rather than for the convenience of Indian travellers.

Japan's railways were built after the Meiji Restoration in 1868, when the government decided to modernise the country and to adopt Western technology. The first line, between Shimbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama, opened on 14 October 1872, with locomotives and rolling stock imported from Britain. The Japanese government hired British engineers, and it trained Japanese engineers to build and maintain the lines. Japan's railways spread rapidly, and by the end of the century the country had a national network. Japanese engineers later became leaders in railway design, and Japan's railways would eventually produce the world's first high-speed trains.

China's railways had a more troubled start. The Chinese government initially resisted railway construction, and the first line, a short British-built track between Shanghai and Wusong, opened in 1876 and was bought and dismantled by the Chinese government in 1877. Railways were built later, often with foreign investment and under foreign concessions, and the Chinese state did not gain a unified system until the twentieth century. The railways of China became a focus of political conflict, and their development was shaped by the foreign powers that controlled them. After 1949, the People's Republic of China rebuilt and expanded its network, and it went on to develop the largest high-speed rail system in the world.

The Ottoman Empire built the Hejaz Railway between 1900 and 1908, a line from Damascus to Medina intended to carry pilgrims and to strengthen imperial control over the Arabian interior. It was a remarkable project in a hostile terrain, and parts of it survive as a heritage railway. The Hejaz Railway was damaged during the First World War and was never completed to its original plan, but it showed that the railway could serve religious and political purposes as well as economic ones.

In Africa, railways were built to serve mining and colonial administration. The Cape Government Railways began in the 1850s and 1860s, and the lines spread from Cape Town into the interior, carrying diamonds and later gold and coal. The most famous colonial line was the Cape to Cairo project, which was envisioned by British imperialists but never completed as a single route. Lines were built in Egypt, Sudan, Kenya, and Uganda, often to serve the needs of colonial governments and European settlers. The network that emerged was fragmented, with different gauges and separate administrations in each territory. After independence, African governments inherited these networks, and many of them struggled to maintain and expand the lines.

Australia built its railways in the colonial period, and the gauges chosen by the colonies differed from one another. Victoria and New South Wales adopted the standard gauge, while Queensland and South Australia built narrower lines. The first Australian railway, the Melbourne and Hobson's Bay Railway, opened in 1854 between Melbourne and Port Melbourne. The gauge differences created problems that were not resolved until the twentieth century, when the lines were standardised. The Australian experience shows, once again, that the decision to build lines to different standards in neighbouring territories could impose long-lasting costs.

## The Steam Locomotive at Its Height

By the late nineteenth century, the steam locomotive had matured into a sophisticated machine. Engineers had learned how to build boilers that produced large volumes of steam at high pressure, how to design cylinders and valves that used steam efficiently, and how to arrange wheels and frames to carry heavy loads at high speed. The steam locomotive became a complex machine with many variations, each suited to particular conditions. Freight engines had large numbers of driving wheels to haul heavy trains slowly up gradients, while passenger engines had large driving wheels and fewer axles to achieve high speeds on the level.

Compound locomotives, which used steam twice by passing it from a high-pressure cylinder to a low-pressure cylinder, improved fuel efficiency and were widely adopted in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The articulated locomotive, in which two sets of driving wheels were mounted on a flexible frame, was developed by Anatole Mallet in the 1880s and was used to haul heavy trains on lines with sharp curves and steep gradients. The Mallet type was popular in mountain regions and in colonial railways, and it allowed engines to be built with great power on lightweight track.

Speed records became a point of national pride. In Britain, the streamlined *Mallard*, designed by Nigel Gresley and built for the London and North Eastern Railway, set a steam locomotive speed record of 126 miles per hour (about 203 km/h) on 3 July 1938, a record that has never been surpassed for steam traction. The Americans built enormous freight and passenger engines, including the Union Pacific Big Boys, which were articulated locomotives designed for the steep grades of the Wasatch Mountains. In Germany, the Prussian railways developed standard designs for passenger and freight traffic, and the standardisation of locomotive types made maintenance more efficient across large networks.

Steam was also the dominant technology in the early twentieth century, and it carried most of the world's passengers and freight. Railways were the largest consumers of coal in many countries, and the coal trade and the railway were closely linked. Steam engines were dirty and required constant maintenance, but they were robust, relatively simple, and capable of running on a wide variety of fuels. Their reliance on coal and water shaped the layout of railways, with depots and water towers placed at intervals along the line, and with turntables and coaling stations at major terminals.

The First World War placed great demands on railways. Armies depended on trains to move men, guns, and supplies to the front, and the railway's capacity became a measure of military power. The war also showed the vulnerability of railways to attack, as lines and bridges were bombed or sabotaged, and locomotives were destroyed. After the war, many countries rebuilt their networks, and some, including the United States, returned to private ownership of railways. Britain, which had taken control of its railways during the war, returned them to the companies, though the grouping of 1923 created a more consolidated structure.

The interwar years saw the development of streamlined trains, which were designed to reduce air resistance and to present a modern image to the public. The Burlington Zephyr, a diesel-electric train built in 1934, was one of the first streamlined trains in the United States, and it set speed records on its maiden runs. The streamlined steam locomotives of the 1930s, such as the German *Flying Hamburger* diesel railcars and the British streamlined Pacifics, were marketed as symbols of progress. They gave the public a sense that the railway was keeping pace with the automobile and the airplane, which were increasingly competing for traffic.

## Electric Traction

Electric traction was an idea that predated the steam locomotive. Experiments with electric motors on rails were made in the 1830s and 1840s, and by the late nineteenth century, engineers had developed direct current motors powerful enough to drive trams and small trains. The first electric railways were often small, experimental lines, and they were built to demonstrate what electricity could do. Werner von Siemens built an electric railway at the Berlin Trade Exhibition of 1879, which carried passengers around a short circuit powered by a central generator. In 1881 Siemens opened the Lichterfelde tramway in Berlin, which carried passengers in regular service and is often cited as the first electric tramway in the world.

Volk's Electric Railway, opened in 1883 in Brighton, England, is the oldest operating electric railway in the world. It was built along the seafront and carried passengers for pleasure, not transport. The line's engineer, Magnus Volk, was a pioneer of seaside electric railways, and his line still runs, though it has been modernised many times. Electric trams spread quickly in cities across Europe and North America in the 1890s, and they transformed urban transport by carrying large numbers of passengers at speeds greater than horse-drawn omnibuses could achieve.

Frank Sprague, an American engineer, played a leading role in the development of electric traction. His electric trams in Richmond, Virginia, which began operation in 1888, demonstrated that electric motors could be controlled reliably and that a system of trams could be operated at a profit. Sprague developed the multiple unit control system, which allowed several motors on different cars to be operated from a single controller, making it possible to build long trains with electric power. This innovation became the basis for electric commuter trains and rapid transit systems, and it is still used today.

Electric urban railways led to the first underground railways. The City and South London Railway, opened in 1890, was the first deep-level underground electric railway in the world. It used tunnels bored through London clay, and its small carriages were hauled by electric locomotives. The line was a success, and it demonstrated that electric traction could work underground, where steam engines produced smoke and fumes that were intolerable in enclosed spaces. The London Underground grew from this beginning, and other cities built their own underground systems in the following decades.

The Liverpool Overhead Railway, opened in 1893, was one of the first electric elevated railways, carrying passengers along the docks above the streets. It used electric traction from the start, and it was a model for later elevated systems in the United States and Europe. In New York and Chicago, elevated railways were built in the 1870s and 1880s, initially steam-powered, and then electrified in the 1890s, transforming the urban transport of those cities.

Main line electrification was slower, because the cost of building the infrastructure was high and the benefits were not always clear. Direct current at moderate voltages was suitable for urban systems, but it was difficult to transmit over long distances without losses. The development of alternating current systems and of high-voltage transmission made it possible to supply long-distance railways with power from distant generating stations. Single-phase alternating current, which was used in some European and American systems, allowed the use of high voltages on the overhead wire while keeping the motors simple and efficient.

In the United States, the Pennsylvania Railroad built an electric system to serve its terminal in New York in the early twentieth century, including a tunnel under the Hudson River and an electric service into Manhattan. The electrification of the New York approaches was among the largest projects of its kind, and it used direct current at moderate voltage. The Pennsylvania's lines were a showcase for electric traction, and they demonstrated that electric trains could serve heavy commuter traffic reliably.

In Italy, Switzerland, Sweden, and Austria, electrification was pursued for different reasons. Switzerland had abundant hydroelectric power, and its railways were electrified to reduce dependence on imported coal. The Gotthard line through the Alps was electrified in the early twentieth century, and it was one of the first long mountain lines to use electric traction. The Swedish line from Kiruna to the iron ore port at Narvik was electrified in the 1910s, and it carried iron ore out of the Arctic on a route that had few alternatives. Electrification in these countries was driven by the need for power on steep gradients and in regions with limited fuel.

After the Second World War, electrification became standard practice on busy European routes, especially in France and Germany. France adopted a 25 kilovolt 50 hertz alternating current system for its main lines, and Germany used 15 kilovolt 16⅔ hertz, a legacy of its early adoption of single-phase traction. These two systems were incompatible with one another, which created problems for international trains, and they are still present in many parts of Europe. The European Union later adopted standards for interoperability, and multi-system locomotives became common as a way to cross borders without changing engines.

## The Diesel Revolution

The diesel engine was invented by Rudolf Diesel in the 1890s, and it was first applied to locomotives in the early twentieth century. A diesel engine uses compression ignition rather than spark ignition, and it can achieve higher efficiency than a steam engine. Early diesel locomotives were built as mechanical transmissions, but the diesel-electric system, in which a diesel engine drives an electric generator that supplies power to electric traction motors, proved more practical for locomotives. The diesel-electric locomotive could be controlled easily, it could be made in modular units, and it could run on a wide range of track conditions.

The first successful diesel-electric locomotives were built in the 1920s and 1930s, and they were used first for switching and shunting in yards, where the low speed and frequent starts made the advantages of diesel obvious. Diesel did not need water or coal, and it could be left idle without the expense of banking fires. The American locomotive builders, especially the Electro-Motive Division of General Motors, developed a line of diesel-electric locomotives that became widely used in the United States. The EMD F-units of the 1940s became the standard passenger and freight locomotives of American railroads, and they replaced steam engines across much of the country within a few years of the Second World War.

The shift from steam to diesel in the United States was remarkably fast. By the early 1950s, most American railroads were dieselising their operations, and by the end of the decade steam had almost disappeared from the main lines. The reasons were economic: diesel locomotives required less maintenance, they were more efficient in fuel use when measured by the cost of running and maintaining them, and they could operate for longer periods between servicing. The change also reflected the growth of competition from trucks and automobiles, which pressured the railroads to cut costs and improve speed.

Britain changed more slowly. The British Railways Modernisation Plan of 1955 called for the replacement of steam by diesel and electric traction over a period of about fifteen years. The plan was ambitious and expensive, and it was not always well managed. Some early diesel locomotives were unreliable, and the decision to build electric and diesel traction in many variants created problems of standardisation. Even so, steam was gradually withdrawn from service, and the last steam trains ran on British Railways in August 1968. Steam continued on some heritage railways and on some preserved lines, and it remains a popular attraction for enthusiasts.

Diesel traction also brought a change in passenger experience. Diesel multiple units, in which several cars were powered by diesel engines built into the carriage, were used on secondary routes and on commuter lines. They were quieter and cleaner than steam trains, and they allowed frequent services on routes with modest traffic. The diesel railcar became a common sight across Europe and North America, and it kept many branch lines open that might otherwise have closed.

The diesel locomotive also changed the economics of freight. Diesel engines could haul heavier trains, run longer distances without refuelling, and be controlled from multiple units at the head and tail of a train. The change made it possible to run longer trains and to reduce the number of crews needed for a given volume of freight. The consolidation of freight traffic into unit trains, which carried a single commodity between fixed points, was made possible by the capabilities of diesel and electric locomotives.

## Decline, Competition, and Renewal

The decline of the railway in many countries after the Second World War was a result of several forces. The automobile and the highway offered flexibility and door-to-door service that the railway could not match, and the building of motorways in the 1950s and 1960s drew traffic away from trains. Air travel offered speed on long-distance routes, and airlines competed directly with trains between major cities. Governments subsidised roads and airports more generously than railways, and the railway's share of passenger and freight traffic fell in many countries.

In Britain, the decline was dramatic. The Beeching Report of 1963, produced by Richard Beeching, recommended the closure of many branch lines and unprofitable routes, and it led to the withdrawal of thousands of miles of track. Many of the lines were in rural areas, and their closure caused lasting damage to local communities. Some of the closed lines were later reopened or converted into footpaths and cycleways, and some were restored as heritage railways. The Beeching cuts became a symbol of the decline of rail in Britain, and they remain a point of debate.

In the United States, the railroads faced a severe crisis in the 1960s and early 1970s. Passenger services declined rapidly, and many lines were abandoned. The Penn Central, formed by the merger of the Pennsylvania Railroad and the New York Central in 1968, went bankrupt in June 1970. The bankruptcy led the federal government to create Amtrak, a national passenger railway corporation, which began operating on 1 May 1971. The Consolidated Rail Corporation, known as Conrail, was created in 1976 to take over the bankrupt Northeast lines. The Staggers Rail Act of 1980 deregulated freight railroads, allowing them to set rates and to abandon unprofitable lines more easily. Freight railroads recovered in the following decades, and the American freight system became one of the most efficient in the world, though passenger rail remained small.

The growth of containerisation transformed freight. Standard containers, introduced in the 1950s and 1960s, could be loaded onto ships, trains, and trucks without being opened, and they linked the modes of transport together. Intermodal rail, in which containers were carried by train over long distances, became a major part of the freight business. In the United States, double-stack container trains, in which containers were stacked two high on railcars, were introduced in the 1980s, and they increased the capacity of freight lines dramatically.

Railways in Europe responded to competition in a different way. Governments in many countries saw the railway as a public service that should be protected from the full pressures of the market. Subsidies kept many lines open, and national railways were reorganised and modernised. The idea of a high-speed railway, which could compete with air travel on routes of a few hundred kilometres, became a central part of this response. The success of high-speed rail in Japan, France, and Germany showed that a railway could regain passengers from airlines and cars if it could offer speed, comfort, and frequency.

## The Shinkansen and the Birth of High-Speed Rail

The modern era of high-speed rail began in Japan. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen, a line between Tokyo and Osaka, opened on 1 October 1964, in time for the Tokyo Olympics. It was a remarkable achievement, built to a standard gauge of 1,435 millimetres rather than the narrower gauge used on most Japanese lines, and it was designed to operate at a top speed of 210 kilometres per hour. The line was built on new alignments, with few level crossings and with a separate track for high-speed trains, and it was designed for frequent service. The Shinkansen reduced the journey time between Tokyo and Osaka to about three hours and ten minutes, a dramatic improvement that drew passengers away from the airlines and the older express trains.

The Shinkansen was not simply a faster train. It was a system that combined new infrastructure, new rolling stock, and new operating practices. The track was carefully built, with continuously welded rails, and the line was equipped with automatic train control and with a system that detected earthquakes and stopped trains if a dangerous tremor occurred. The Shinkansen's safety record has been exceptional. In more than half a century of operation, no passenger has been killed in a derailment or collision on the Shinkansen network, a record that has been widely celebrated. The line's punctuality has also been remarkable, with trains often leaving and arriving to the minute.

The Shinkansen's success led to a rapid expansion. The Sanyō Shinkansen extended the line west to Hakata in Kyushu, and the Tōhoku and Jōetsu Shinkansen extended it north to Tokyo's northern regions in the 1980s. The Hokuriku Shinkansen followed, along with other lines that connected much of the country. Japan's high-speed network became one of the most extensive in the world, and it carried millions of passengers every day. The Shinkansen also became a symbol of Japanese technological achievement, and it was a point of national pride.

The Japanese system also produced a new generation of trains. The 0 Series Shinkansen, which entered service in 1964, was the first of a long line of high-speed trains, and later series introduced improvements in aerodynamics, noise reduction, and passenger comfort. The nose shapes of later Shinkansen trains were designed to reduce noise when they emerged from tunnels, an issue that became serious as speeds increased. Engineers studied the aerodynamics of train noise closely, and the resulting designs were copied in other countries.

## The TGV and European High Speed

France was the next major country to build a high-speed railway. The Train à Grande Vitesse, or TGV, was developed by the French national railway company SNCF in the 1970s and entered service in 1981 on a new line between Paris and Lyon. The line was built on new track designed for speeds of up to 300 kilometres per hour, and the trains were powered by electric traction at 25 kilovolts. The TGV reduced the journey time between Paris and Lyon from about four hours to a little under two, and it helped establish high-speed rail as a major competitor to air travel and car travel on routes of several hundred kilometres.

The TGV was designed with a distinctive articulated layout, in which pairs of carriages shared a single bogie at their joint. This arrangement reduced the weight of the train and improved its stability at high speed. The trains had power cars at each end, and they could be coupled together to form longer trains for busy routes. The TGV was also quiet and smooth, and its carriages were comfortable, with a level of refinement that drew positive comment from travellers.

The TGV set a world speed record for conventional wheel-on-rail trains on 18 May 1990, when a specially prepared TGV Atlantique reached 515.3 kilometres per hour on a test section of the new line between Paris and Le Mans. The record was a demonstration of what the technology could do, and it helped establish France's position as a leader in high-speed rail. The TGV network grew steadily, with new lines serving Lille, the Atlantic coast, the Mediterranean, the Alps, and eastern France. The TGV was exported to other countries, and its design influenced trains built elsewhere.

Germany built its own high-speed network in the 1990s, and the Intercity-Express, or ICE, began service in 1991. The German system was based on new lines and on the upgrading of existing routes, and it was developed in parallel with the French system. The ICE trains used a different design from the TGV, with a conventional locomotive-hauled layout in the first generation and later with distributed power in subsequent generations. The German network became one of the largest high-speed systems in Europe, linking major cities across the country.

Spain built its high-speed network in the early 1990s, and the Madrid to Seville line opened in April 1992, in time for the Seville Expo. The Spanish high-speed system used a broad gauge different from the standard gauge of the TGV and ICE, which meant that Spanish trains could not run directly onto the French network. Spain later built lines that connected with the French system at the border, and it developed trains that could run on both gauges. The Spanish network became the largest in Europe, with lines radiating from Madrid to much of the country.

The opening of the Channel Tunnel in 1994 made it possible to run high-speed trains between London and Paris and Brussels. The Eurostar service began in the same year, and it linked the British and French capitals with trains that travelled through the tunnel at high speed. The British high-speed line, which was built as a new link from the tunnel into London, was completed in 2007 and opened to trains that could run at 300 kilometres per hour on the section from the tunnel. The Eurostar was a commercial success, and it drew passengers away from airlines on the London to Paris route.

The European high-speed network grew steadily, and by the early twenty-first century it had become a major part of the continent's transport system. Italy built lines from Turin to Milan, and from Milan to Rome and Naples, with trains that competed with air and road travel. The Netherlands, Belgium, and Switzerland built lines that linked their cities with each other and with neighbouring countries. The European Union worked to establish common standards for signalling and interoperability, through the European Rail Traffic Management System and the European Train Control System, so that trains could cross borders without changing equipment. These systems are still being implemented, and they have been slow to replace the older national systems in many countries.

## China and the Expansion of High-Speed Rail

China became the world's leading builder of high-speed rail in the early twenty-first century. The country's first high-speed lines were built for the Beijing Olympics, and the Beijing to Tianjin line opened in August 2008, with trains designed for speeds of up to 350 kilometres per hour. The Wuhan to Guangzhou line, which opened in December 2009, was one of the first long-distance high-speed lines in China, and it was followed by a rapid expansion of the network. By the mid-2020s, China had built well over forty thousand kilometres of high-speed line, which is more than the rest of the world combined.

The Chinese high-speed network was built with extraordinary speed. Government planning, state-owned construction companies, and large-scale investment made it possible to build lines quickly across varied terrain, including mountains, deserts, and river valleys. The trains were built by Chinese manufacturers, who initially cooperated with foreign companies to acquire technology and later developed their own designs. The Chinese network carries hundreds of millions of passengers every year, and it has changed the travel patterns of many regions. Cities that were once days apart by train are now a few hours apart, and business and tourism have shifted accordingly.

The expansion of Chinese high-speed rail has also raised questions. Some lines have been criticised for low ridership relative to their cost, and debt associated with the construction of the network has been a concern. The 2011 Wenzhou collision, in which two high-speed trains collided and killed dozens of people, led to a review of safety and signalling, and it drew attention to the risks of rapid expansion. The Chinese government responded by improving safety systems and by slowing the pace of new construction for a time, and it has since resumed building. The Chinese case shows that high-speed rail can be built at great scale, but that its economic and safety performance depends on careful management.

Chinese high-speed trains have also influenced global markets. Chinese manufacturers have exported trains to several countries, and they have competed for contracts in Southeast Asia, Africa, and Europe. The competition has been fierce, and it has pushed prices down and encouraged other manufacturers to develop cheaper designs. The Chinese success has changed the perception of high-speed rail as a technology dominated by Japan, France, and Germany.

## Other High-Speed Systems

High-speed rail has spread to many other countries. South Korea built its KTX network in the 2000s, using French technology in the initial stages and later developing domestic trains. Taiwan built a high-speed line between Taipei and Kaohsiung in the 2000s, using Japanese technology. Turkey built high-speed lines linking Ankara with Istanbul and other cities, and several other countries in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East have built or planned lines. Saudi Arabia's Haramain line, which opened in 2018, connects Mecca, Medina, and Jeddah, and it carries pilgrims and travellers at speeds of up to 300 kilometres per hour on the sections designed for that speed.

Indonesia opened its first high-speed line, the Jakarta to Bandung route, in 2023. The line was built with Chinese technology and financing, and it was among the first high-speed railways in Southeast Asia. The project was affected by delays and cost overruns, and its economic success has been debated. It nevertheless showed that high-speed rail was becoming a truly global technology, available to countries outside the wealthy industrial core.

The United States has no high-speed rail network in the sense that the term is used elsewhere. The Northeast Corridor, between Boston, New York, and Washington, carries high-speed trains at speeds of up to 150 miles per hour on some sections, but most of the route is limited by older track and by curves that prevent full speeds. California has been building a high-speed railway since the 2010s, linking the Central Valley with the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles. The project has faced repeated political and financial challenges, and its completion has been pushed back several times, but construction has continued on sections in the Central Valley.

The United Kingdom has discussed high-speed rail since the early 2000s. The High Speed 1 line was completed in 2007 and connected London with the Channel Tunnel. The High Speed 2 project, intended to link London with the Midlands, the North, and Scotland, was approved in stages in the 2010s, but it has been scaled back. In 2023, the government cancelled the planned section between the West Midlands and Leeds, and the project's future has been uncertain. The British experience illustrates the difficulty of building major infrastructure in a country with dense development, complex planning procedures, and fluctuating political priorities.

## Maglev and the Future of Speed

Magnetic levitation, or maglev, offers a different approach to high-speed travel. Maglev trains float above a guideway, supported by magnetic forces, and they are propelled by linear motors that create a moving magnetic field. Without wheels touching the track, maglev trains avoid the friction that limits the speed of conventional trains, and they can reach very high speeds with relatively little noise and vibration. The technology has been developed in Germany, Japan, China, and other countries, and it has been demonstrated at high speeds in testing.

The Transrapid system, developed in Germany, was the first maglev to carry passengers in regular service. A line in Shanghai, opened in 2004, connects the city's airport with the edge of its financial district, a distance of about thirty kilometres. The line reaches speeds of about 430 kilometres per hour in operation, making it one of the fastest commercial trains in the world. The Shanghai maglev has been criticised for its high cost and limited route, and it has not been extended as originally planned, but it has shown that maglev can operate safely and reliably in daily service.

Japan has developed the SCMaglev, which uses superconducting magnets to achieve higher levitation and speed. In December 2015, a test train on the Yamanashi test line reached 603 kilometres per hour, a world record for a rail vehicle. Japan plans to build a maglev line, the Chūō Shinkansen, between Tokyo and Nagoya, and later to Osaka. The project has faced delays and cost increases, and its opening has been postponed to the 2030s or later. The Chūō Shinkansen would be the first commercial superconducting maglev line, and it would show whether the technology can be built and operated economically on a large scale.

Maglev has been difficult to commercialise because of its cost. Building a new guideway for maglev requires a different infrastructure from conventional rail, and the trains themselves are complex and expensive. Conventional high-speed rail, which uses existing technology and standard tracks, has been more successful in attracting investment and passengers. Maglev may find its niche on routes that are very long, very busy, or very constrained by terrain, but its future is still uncertain.

Other proposals have sought even higher speeds. The Hyperloop concept, promoted in the 2010s, envisaged passenger capsules travelling through low-pressure tubes at very high speeds. The concept attracted much attention and some investment, but it has not yet produced a working passenger system. Engineers have raised questions about cost, safety, and the difficulty of building and maintaining long vacuum tubes, and no major operator has committed to the technology. The Hyperloop is a reminder that the search for speed often produces ambitious proposals that are difficult to realise.

## Signalling, Control, and the Invisible Railway

The safety and capacity of the railway depend as much on signalling and control systems as on the trains themselves. Early railways used simple methods to keep trains apart: a train could be sent only when the previous one had cleared the section, and signals were operated by hand. The introduction of the electric telegraph in the 1840s allowed signalmen to communicate with each other over long distances, and it made possible the block system, in which a line was divided into sections and only one train was allowed in each section at a time. The block system became the foundation of railway safety, and it is still in use in some form.

Mechanical interlocking, in which the levers controlling signals and points were mechanically linked so that conflicting routes could not be set, was developed in the nineteenth century and became standard at busy junctions and stations. The interlocking system prevented signalmen from setting a route that would cause a collision, and it reduced the risk of human error. Later, electrical interlocking replaced mechanical systems in many places, and it allowed signal boxes to control large areas of track from a single location.

Automatic train protection systems were developed to prevent trains from passing signals at danger. The early systems used trackside equipment to warn drivers and to stop trains if they failed to respond. The development of more advanced systems, including cab signalling and continuous automatic train control, provided drivers with real-time information about the speed limits ahead and the state of the signals. The European Train Control System, part of the European Rail Traffic Management System, is designed to provide a common standard across national networks, and it is being installed on many European lines.

The introduction of computer-based control has transformed signalling in many places. Communications-based train control, or CBTC, uses radio links between trains and control centres to determine train positions and to manage movements. It allows trains to run closer together and to achieve higher capacity than traditional fixed-block systems. CBTC is widely used on urban metro systems and is being adopted on some main lines. The development of satellite positioning and digital communication has further changed railway operations, and it is making possible new approaches to train control.

The railway's invisible systems include power supply, communications, and maintenance. Modern railways depend on electrical supply systems, substations, overhead wires or third rails, and signalling power. They also depend on track geometry measurement, which uses specialised trains to detect faults in rails and ballast, and on condition monitoring of trains, which uses sensors to detect problems before they cause failures. These systems have made railways safer and more reliable, but they also make the network more complex and more dependent on software and data.

## Bridges, Tunnels, and the Engineering of the Route

The railway's engineering is visible in its bridges and tunnels, and these structures have often been among the most ambitious works of their age. Early railway bridges were built of stone, brick, and cast iron, and they were designed to carry the weight of heavy trains on relatively short spans. The development of wrought iron and then steel made possible longer spans and lighter structures, and engineers built a series of remarkable bridges in the late nineteenth century.

The Forth Bridge, opened in Scotland in 1890, is one of the most famous cantilever bridges in the world. It was designed by John Fowler and Benjamin Baker to carry the main line between Edinburgh and the north across the Firth of Forth. The bridge was built of steel, and its cantilevers reached far across the water. It was an enormous undertaking, and it used more steel than any previous structure. It remains in use today, and it is a World Heritage Site.

Tunnels were equally challenging. The Mont Cenis Tunnel, between France and Italy, was begun in 1857 and completed in 1871, and it was one of the first great Alpine rail tunnels. It was bored using compressed-air drills and was among the first large projects to use mechanical drilling. The Gotthard Tunnel, completed in 1882, carried the railway through the Swiss Alps, and it was one of the longest railway tunnels of its time. The Simplon Tunnel, completed in 1905, was longer still, and it linked Switzerland with Italy at a lower altitude than the earlier tunnels.

The Seikan Tunnel, completed in Japan in 1988, is the longest railway tunnel in the world, with a total length of about 53.85 kilometres, most of it beneath the seabed. The tunnel was built to carry trains between Honshu and Hokkaido, and it was intended to overcome the difficulties of crossing the Tsugaru Strait. The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, is the longest undersea tunnel in the world, and it carries both passenger and freight trains between England and France. Its construction was a major achievement, and its operation has shown that railway traffic can cross the English Channel safely and quickly.

Engineers have also developed techniques for building in difficult terrain. In mountains, railways use spiral tunnels, switchbacks, and zigzags to gain height without excessive gradients. In deserts, they use long embankments and ballast to cope with sand and heat. In permafrost, they use foundations designed to avoid thawing and settling. The engineering of railways shows the ingenuity of engineers in overcoming obstacles that would have stopped earlier generations of travellers.

## Freight, Logistics, and the Economy of the Railway

Railways have always been as much about freight as about passengers. The first railways were built to carry coal, iron, and stone, and freight has remained a large part of the railway business in many countries. The railway is particularly efficient for carrying heavy bulk goods over long distances, because its steel wheels on steel rails offer very low rolling resistance, and because a single locomotive can haul hundreds of wagons. A freight train can carry as much as dozens of lorries, using far less fuel per tonne-kilometre.

Bulk freight remains important. Coal, iron ore, grain, and cement are still carried by rail in large quantities in many countries. Unit trains, which carry a single commodity between two points without stopping to switch wagons, are used to move coal from mines to power stations and iron ore from mines to ports. Heavy haul railways in Australia, Brazil, and North America carry massive volumes of ore and coal, and they are among the most productive freight systems in the world.

Containerisation has transformed freight logistics. Standard containers can be moved by ship, rail, and road without being opened, which reduces handling costs and speeds delivery. Intermodal terminals, where containers are transferred between trains and trucks, have become important nodes in the transport system. Container trains carry goods from ports to inland distribution centres, and they link global supply chains with national markets. The growth of container traffic has made rail freight more competitive with road transport over long distances.

The economics of railway freight depend heavily on the quality of infrastructure and the efficiency of operations. A railway with good track, strong bridges, and modern signalling can carry more freight at higher speed and lower cost. A railway with poor track, weak bridges, and old signals will struggle to attract freight. In many countries, governments have invested in freight corridors and in improvements to key routes to make rail more competitive.

Passenger and freight traffic compete for capacity on many lines. High-speed passenger trains need dedicated tracks or carefully scheduled paths, and freight trains are slower and heavier, which makes mixing them difficult. Many railways have built separate freight lines or bypasses to avoid conflicts, and some have moved freight to off-peak hours. The allocation of capacity between passengers and freight is one of the central problems of railway management.

## The Railway and Society

The railway has changed society in ways that go far beyond transport. It made possible the growth of large cities, the suburbanisation of commuting, and the spread of national markets. It allowed the distribution of newspapers and mail, and it made possible the rapid spread of information. It changed the way people thought about distance and time, and it created new forms of work, from the railway clerk to the engine driver and the signalman.

The railway also created new forms of social life. Stations became public spaces, with waiting rooms, shops, and restaurants, and they often became the focal points of cities. The railway carried soldiers to war and brought families together, and it made tourism possible for people who had never travelled far from home. The seaside resort, the mountain hotel, and the spa town all owed much of their growth to the railway.

Railway workers formed some of the earliest large trade unions and social organisations. The discipline of railway work, with its timetables, shifts, and safety rules, required a new kind of organisation, and railway companies developed hierarchies of management that influenced the development of modern corporations. The railway's need for accurate timekeeping and standardised procedures made it a model for other industries.

Railways have also been associated with social and political conflict. Strikes, mass protests, and nationalisation debates have shaped the history of many countries. The question of who should own and operate the railway, and in whose interests it should be run, has been a continual theme. In some countries, railways were nationalised early and operated as public services; in others they remained in private hands for much longer. The balance between public and private ownership has changed over time, and it continues to shape policy debates.

Railways have also been implicated in some of the darkest chapters of modern history. Railway networks were used to transport prisoners and deportees in the twentieth century, and rail systems played a central role in the logistics of forced deportation and genocide. The railway's capacity to move large numbers of people has made it a powerful instrument of both freedom and coercion. Remembering this history is part of understanding the railway's place in society.

## Environment, Energy, and Climate

Railways are often described as environmentally friendly, and in many respects they are. Rail transport uses less energy per passenger-kilometre and per tonne-kilometre than road or air transport, and it produces fewer emissions per unit of traffic when electrified and powered by low-carbon electricity. Electric trains running on renewable power are among the cleanest forms of mechanised transport. Railways also occupy less land per passenger than motorways and airports, and they can carry large numbers of people through dense urban areas without the congestion of road traffic.

The environmental benefits of railways depend on how they are run and powered. Diesel trains produce emissions and noise, and they are less efficient than electric trains. Electrification requires substantial investment in infrastructure, and its benefits depend on the source of electricity. A country that generates most of its power from coal will not achieve the same environmental gains from electric trains as one that uses hydroelectric, wind, or solar power. Railways in many countries are working to decarbonise their operations through electrification, battery traction, and hydrogen trains.

High-speed rail is often promoted as a way to reduce air travel and its emissions. On routes of a few hundred kilometres, a high-speed train can compete with aircraft on time and cost, and it produces far fewer emissions per passenger. Where high-speed rail has replaced air services, as in parts of France, Spain, and Japan, the environmental benefits have been real. However, high-speed rail requires large construction investment and substantial land, and the environmental impact of building new lines must be weighed against the benefits of operation.

The climate debate has encouraged governments to consider rail more seriously. Investment in rail has been promoted as part of programmes to reduce emissions, and some countries have adopted policies to shift freight from road to rail. The railway's role in the future of transport depends on political choices, economic conditions, and technological development, and it remains a matter of debate.
